digest.tldr: Prostate RT led the day: HYPO-RT-PC gives randomised support for 7-fx UHF, though the upper CI bound sits just under the NI margin; 70 Gy/28 fx IMRT holds 10-yr late G≥3 GU 2%, GI 1%; RTOG 0415 modeling sets rectal D5% ≤62 Gy for 10% late ≥G2 GI in low-risk pts. Breast: crude LRR 4.7% without PMRT in high-risk T1-T2N0.

studies.name: NRG/RTOG 0415 late toxicity tolerance doses
studies.tldr: Rectal D5% (EQD2) ≤62 Gy predicted halving late ≥G2 GI toxicity from 20% to 10% after 70 Gy at 2.5 Gy/fx in low-risk prostate cancer.

details.text: 🔍 Secondary dose-volume analysis of the HRT arm of NRG/RTOG 0415, low-risk prostate cancer, N=521

details: 💊 RT: 70 Gy at 2.5 Gy/fraction, 3DCRT/IMRT N=108/413

details.text: 🔍 Median f/u 5.9 yr; crude late ≥G2 GI 19%, GU 29%
🔍 Random 70%/30% training/validation split; logistic NTCP models on bootstrapping, EQD2 with rectum α/β 3 Gy, bladder 6 Gy
📐 Two generalizable GI models (D5% ± acute GI tox): AUCvalidation 0.64 and 0.65, p=0.01 and 0.03, pHL 0.45-0.56
📊 Rectal D5%[Gy] (EQD2) thresholds by target late ≥G2 GI rate

columns: D5% if acute GI tox (Model II)

details.text: 📊 Proctitis: observed 14% at D5% 64 Gy; ≤63 Gy for 10%; 62 Gy limit modeled to 7%
📊 GU: no dose-response for bladder; acute GU tox only a trend (AUCtraining 0.57, p=0.07)
⚠️ Rectal V74Gy[%] ≤15 constraint adherence only 84% overall, 77% among pts with late GI tox
⚠️ Discrimination modest (AUC 0.64-0.65); proctitis model only approached significance in validation (p=0.07)

details: ⚠️ Single-arm subset of one trial, IMRT-heavy cohort; technique effect could not be resolved

details.text: 🔗 Parent trial: HRT vs CFRT late ≥G2 GI 22% vs 20% (p=0.005), GU 26% vs 21% (p=0.009)

verdict.rationale: Post-hoc NTCP modeling within one arm of a phase III; modest AUC 0.64-0.65, internal split validation only, no prospective test of the proposed D5% constraint.
verdict.audience: Low-risk prostate cancer, HRT arm of NRG/RTOG 0415

studies.significance: The constraint that matters is a small-volume hotspot, not the high-dose V74Gy rule, which 16% of plans missed anyway. Pts with acute GI toxicity have a lower modeled tolerance (D5% ≤55 Gy for a 10% late GI rate), so planning targets may need to differ by acute course. Bladder dose explained nothing for GU, pointing elsewhere for mitigation.
studies.monday_clinic: In low-risk prostate cancer planned for moderate HRT at 2.5 Gy/fx, this supports adding a rectal D5% (EQD2) ceiling near 62 Gy as a GI-toxicity planning goal; it does not inform GU toxicity, where no bladder dose-response emerged.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Secondary dose-volume analysis of the **HRT arm** of the multicenter NRG/RTOG 0415 trial, N=521. Cohort split **70%/30%** into training and validation with preserved toxicity rates; univariate and multivariate logistic regression on bootstrapping.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **Low-risk prostate cancer** treated on the HRT arm. Median follow-up **5.9 yr**.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **70 Gy at 2.5 Gy/fraction**, 3DCRT/IMRT N=108/413. Doses converted to EQD2 with rectum α/β 3 Gy and bladder 6 Gy; trial rectal constraint EQD2 74 Gy ≤15%.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Late ≥G2 GI and GU toxicity**, plus proctitis and pollakiuria (the symptoms with rates ≥10%). Generalizability required validation AUC within training AUC ± SD, p≤0.05, and pHL >0.05.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **Rectal D5%** was the dominant GI predictor; with or without acute GI toxicity it generalized (AUCvalidation **0.64, 0.65**). Modeled late GI falls from 20% to 10% at **D5% ≤62 Gy**. **No GU dose-response** was found, including at α/β 0.8 Gy.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: PROFIT, CHHiP, HYPRO and RTOG 0415 established moderate HRT with similar biochemical control to CFRT but a tendency to more late toxicity. The late GI rate here was **19% vs 2%** in a cited high-dose CFRT IMRT series planned with a strict high-dose rectal constraint.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Validation is an internal random split of the same cohort, not an external dataset. The IMRT-heavy mix (**79% vs 21%**) left a technique interaction untestable, and constraint adherence was incomplete, so part of the signal may reflect plan quality rather than tolerance.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents low-risk prostate cancer treated with moderate HRT at 2.5 Gy/fx. Does not represent ultrahypofractionated SBRT, nodal fields, or GU toxicity mitigation.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Results point to small rectal hotspots as the modifiable driver of excess late GI toxicity after moderate HRT, with authors also advocating **rectal spacers**. GU toxicity likely needs a substructure (not whole-bladder) approach.

studies.interpretation:
The HRT trials that moved prostate practice toward moderate hypofractionation, PROFIT, CHHiP, HYPRO and RTOG 0415 among them, settled the efficacy question but left a toxicity residue: late GI and GU events tended to run higher than with conventional fractionation, and in RTOG 0415 the difference reached significance for both domains. The obvious response is better normal-tissue constraints, yet most constraints in use were inherited from conventional schedules. This analysis is one of the few attempts to derive HRT-specific rectal tolerance from prospectively collected trial toxicity, which is its main value.

The finding that matters is where the risk sits in the DVH. The parent trial already carried a high-dose rectal volume constraint, but the model points at the minimum dose to the hottest 5% of rectum rather than the intermediate-dose volumes or the protocol's V74 rule. That is consistent with a hotspot mechanism, and it is clinically convenient: a D5% objective is easy to add to an IMRT optimizer without rewriting the whole constraint set. The other practical point is that adherence to the existing rectal constraint was incomplete, lower still among pts who developed toxicity. Some of the excess late GI risk after HRT may therefore be a plan-quality problem rather than a fractionation problem, and a new number will not fix plans that do not meet the old one.

Confidence should be tempered by the statistics. Discrimination is modest, with validation AUCs of 0.64 and 0.65, which means D5% explains only a fraction of who gets late GI toxicity. Validation was an internal random split of the same 521 pts, so the model was tested on pts planned under the same protocol, the same contouring rules and the same era of IMRT; that is generalizability within a trial, not across practice. The proctitis model only approached significance in validation. The predicted halving of toxicity at D5% 62 Gy is a model extrapolation along a fitted logistic curve over a narrow dose range, not an observed effect of lowering the dose, and the cohort is dominated by IMRT, so any technique effect is unresolved.

The acute-toxicity interaction deserves more attention than it gets. Pts with acute GI toxicity had considerably lower modeled thresholds, which, if real, suggests either individual radiosensitivity or a consequential-late mechanism, and in either case argues that a single constraint is too blunt. It does not yet tell a planner what to do before treatment starts, since acute toxicity is not known at planning.

The null GU result is informative. Late GU toxicity was more common than GI, yet whole-bladder dose explained none of it even with a much lower α/β. That supports looking at urinary substructures rather than tightening bladder constraints. What the analysis cannot answer is whether a D5% objective, applied prospectively and combined with spacers, actually lowers late GI toxicity after moderate HRT; that would require an external or prospective test, and the paper offers none. It is a reasonable, low-cost planning objective to consider, not a validated tolerance.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The constraint that matters is a small-volume rectal hotspot (D5%), not the V74Gy rule that 16% of plans missed anyway. Pts with acute GI toxicity carry lower modeled tolerance (D5% ≤55 Gy for a 10% late GI rate), and bladder dose explained nothing for GU, pointing mitigation toward substructures.

open_questions: Does a prospective D5% ≤62 Gy rectal objective lower late GI toxicity?
Which urinary substructure drives late GU toxicity after HRT?
Does rectal spacer use make the D5% threshold redundant?

studies.name: Moderate hypofractionation 70 Gy/28 fx, 10-year outcomes
studies.tldr: 10-yr bRFS 71%, cRFS 86%, PCSM 6.8% after 70 Gy/28 fx IMRT for localized prostate cancer; late G≥3 GU 2%, GI 1%.

details.text: 🔍 Single-institution series, 854 consecutive pts treated 1998-2012, prospectively maintained registry

details: 🔍 Median f/u 11.3 yr (max 19 yr)

details.text: 🔍 Risk mix: 266 LR, 238 FIR, 106 UIR, 244 HR (NCCN high risk 29%)
🔍 RT technique
subdetails: 70 Gy/28 fx at 2.5 Gy/fx, IMRT in all pts
Authors cite equivalence to 80 Gy in 2 Gy/fx at α/β 1.5
CTV: prostate alone for LR; prostate + proximal SV (≥1 cm) for IR/HR

details.text: 💊 ADT in 61%, mostly 1-6 mo; 18% received >6 mo
📊 10-yr outcomes by risk group (abstract values)
📊 Whole cohort 10-yr OS 69% (95% CI 66%-73%)
📊 Clinical failures 125 (15%): 117 distant metastases, 8 local-only
📊 Late G≥3 toxicity, 10-yr cumulative incidence
subdetails: GU 2% (95% CI 0.8%-3.0%), mostly urethral stricture needing dilatation
Grade 5: 1 GU, 1 GI (rectovesicular fistula, septic death)
Fig 3 read: G≥3 GU 3.7% at 15 yr

details.text: ⚠️ HR bRFS 42% at 10 yr; only 5/244 HR pts received elective pelvic nodal RT

details: ⚠️ Toxicity captured by retrospective chart review, physician-reported, no validated instruments

details.text: ⚠️ Ultrasound-era IGRT and 4-10 mm margins; may not transfer to fiducial/CBCT practice
🔗 vs RTOG 0415 (same 70 Gy/28 fx): authors cite G3 toxicity 3% to 4% at 5 yr, IMRT not mandatory

verdict.rationale: Single-institution nonrandomized cohort without a comparator arm; long follow-up adds durability to randomized hypofractionation data but cannot establish equivalence on its own.
verdict.audience: Localized prostate cancer, all NCCN risk groups, definitive RT ± ADT

studies.significance: Failure after 70 Gy/28 fx was almost entirely distant: 117 of 125 clinical failures were metastatic, 8 local-only. The HR 10-yr bRFS of 42% came with only 5/244 HR pts receiving elective nodal RT, which the authors attribute to short ADT and rare nodal coverage rather than inadequate prostate dose.
studies.monday_clinic: In localized low and intermediate-risk prostate cancer, this supports 70 Gy/28 fx IMRT with daily IGRT as a durable schedule past 10 yr; it does not settle HR disease treated with short ADT and no pelvic nodal RT.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Single-institution consecutive series from a **prospectively maintained registry**, 854 pts treated 1998-2012. **Median follow-up 11.3 yr** (max 19). Not randomized; no comparator arm.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Biopsy-proven, **clinically localized** prostate adenocarcinoma across all NCCN risk groups: 266 LR, 238 FIR, 106 UIR, 244 HR. Median age 68, median PSA 8.6 ng/mL. ADT in **61%**, mostly 1-6 mo.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **70 Gy/28 fx at 2.5 Gy/fx**, IMRT with daily IGRT (BAT ultrasound 94.8%). CTV prostate alone for LR, plus proximal SV for IR/HR; **PTV margin 4-10 mm**. Elective pelvic nodes in only 5 of 244 HR pts.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Whole-cohort 10-yr **bRFS 71%**, **cRFS 86%**, **OS 69%**, **PCSM 6.8%**. Of 125 clinical failures, **117 were distant and 8 local-only**.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: 10-yr late **G≥3 GU 2%** (mostly urethral stricture) and **G≥3 GI 1%** (mostly rectal bleeding). One grade 5 event each in GU and GI. 119 pts (14%) developed a new cancer, lung most common.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Authors place this alongside RTOG 0415, CHHiP, PROFIT, HYPRO and the MDACC series, none with 10-yr outcomes at publication. RTOG 0415 used the same 70 Gy/28 fx with **G3 toxicity 3% to 4% at 5 yr**, under looser dose-volume constraints and without mandatory IMRT.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents localized prostate cancer treated with 70 Gy/28 fx IMRT and daily IGRT at a high-volume center, mostly with short or no ADT. Does not represent HR disease managed with ≥2 yr ADT or elective pelvic nodal RT.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Toxicity was **physician-reported** from retrospective chart review, likely underreporting events. Institutional constraints (rectal/bladder V70 5%, up to 10%) are far tighter than NRG-GU005 allows, so the toxicity rates may not hold under trial or community constraints.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The schedule controls the prostate well over 10+ yr; the risk-group gradient is driven by distant failure. What is left open is whether HR outcomes improve with longer ADT and nodal coverage at this fractionation.

studies.interpretation:
The value of this series lies in its follow-up, not its design. When it was reported, the randomized moderate hypofractionation trials (CHHiP, PROFIT, HYPRO, RTOG 0415) had established non-inferiority at roughly five to six years, and the remaining worry was late: does a 2.5 Gy/fx schedule produce late urethral or rectal injury, or late biochemical failure, after the trials stop reporting? A median of 11.3 years and a maximum near two decades speaks directly to that worry, and the answer here is reassuring. Late G≥3 GU of 2% and GI of 1% at 10 years is at the low end of anything reported for this dose. The figure read of G≥3 GU at 3.7% by 15 years suggests urethral events keep accruing slowly, which matters for a younger pt choosing a schedule.

The oncologic data need to be read through the pattern of failure. Of 125 clinical failures, 117 were distant and 8 were local-only. That is the strongest RT-relevant signal in the paper: at this EQD2 the prostate itself is rarely where the disease comes back. The poor HR result (10-yr bRFS 42%, PCSM 15%) therefore does not argue against the fractionation. It argues that the HR cohort was undertreated by modern standards, with elective nodal RT in only 5 of 244 pts and most ADT courses at 6 months or less. The authors now use at least 2 years of ADT and selectively treat pelvic nodes to 50.4 Gy/28 fx by simultaneous integrated boost, but this paper does not report outcomes with that approach, so the HR numbers should not be quoted as the expected outcome of hypofractionation in HR disease.

Three features should temper confidence in the toxicity figures. First, they were captured by retrospective chart review, physician-reported, without validated instruments; underreporting runs in the favorable direction. Second, the dose constraints are unusually strict: rectal and bladder V70 held to 5% (acceptable to 10%) against NRG-GU005 allowing rectal V70 25% and bladder V70 35%. A center reproducing the schedule under trial or looser constraints should expect rates closer to the 3% to 4% at 5 years the authors cite from RTOG 0415. Third, this is a single high-volume institution with standardized planning, and the authors themselves flag that multi-institutional reproducibility is unclear.

The technical era cuts both ways. Image guidance was ultrasound in 94.8% and PTV margins ran 4 to 10 mm. Modern fiducial or CBCT-based IGRT with tighter margins should lower toxicity further, but it also narrows coverage, and a series dominated by ultrasound alignment cannot tell us whether smaller margins preserve the low local failure rate.

What this changes: little for practice that has already adopted moderate hypofractionation on randomized evidence, but it removes much of the residual concern about late events past the trials' reporting window for low and intermediate-risk localized disease. What it does not settle is the HR question, where the confounding by short ADT and absent nodal coverage makes the outcome data uninformative about the schedule itself.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Failure after 70 Gy/28 fx was almost entirely distant (117 of 125 clinical failures; 8 local-only), so prostate dose is not the HR weak point. Low late toxicity was achieved with rectal/bladder V70 held to 5%, far tighter than NRG-GU005 allows, which gates whether the 2%/1% rates transfer.

open_questions: HR outcomes with 70 Gy/28 fx plus ≥2 yr ADT and pelvic nodal RT
Toxicity reproducibility under looser multi-institutional dose constraints
Whether tighter modern IGRT margins preserve low local failure

studies.name: Integrated clinical-genomic risk groups (Decipher + NCCN)
studies.tldr: 10y DM 3.5%/29.4%/54.6% for clinical-genomic low/int/high vs NCCN 7.3%/9.2%/38.0%/39.5% in localized prostate cancer; 30% reclassified.
details: 🔍 Retrospective development: training n=756 (RP specimens, 1997-2004), validation n=235 (biopsy specimens, 1995-2005)
🔍 Reclassification-only prospective cohorts: n=4,960 (RP) and n=977 (biopsy); no outcome data in these

details.text: 🔍 Point system: NCCN 0-3 + Decipher 0-2 → total 0-5
📊 10y distant metastasis and HR for DM by risk system

details: 📊 NCCN did not separate low from fav-int, or unfav-int from high, for DM in the RP cohort

details.text: 📐 C-index for 10y DM
📊 10y PCSM, clinical-genomic groups (training)
📊 Reclassification vs NCCN in prospective cohorts
subdetails: Cohort I: 56.8% of fav-int and 36.0% of unfav-int reclassified

details: ⚠️ Abstract's c-index 0.84 is the 235-pt validation estimate (CI 0.61-0.93); like-for-like training contrast is 0.77 vs 0.68
⚠️ Treatment-adjusted HRs shrink: CG int 3.5 (1.5-8.3), high 6.1 (2.6-14.4) after adjusting for ADT and RT
⚠️ Validation HRs 21.3 (2.8 to 2,727.6) and 62.5 (8.5 to 7,969.6): sparse events, 0% low-risk DM
⚠️ Prognostic only; no test of whether treatment changes on reclassification alter outcomes
⚠️ Many authors employed by GenomeDx, the Decipher manufacturer

verdict.rationale: Retrospective development with a 235-pt biopsy validation set and sparse low-risk events; prognostic only, no evidence that reclassification-driven treatment changes outcomes.
verdict.audience: Localized prostate cancer, NCCN low to high risk, with Decipher available

studies.significance: The pre-RT setting is the biopsy validation cohort (n=235), where 10y DM ran 0%/25.9%/55.2% across clinical-genomic tiers. The reclassification hits the NCCN favorable/unfavorable intermediate boundary hardest (56.8% and 36.0% moved in prospective cohort I), which is the line that gates adding ADT to RT.
studies.monday_clinic: In NCCN intermediate-risk localized prostate cancer, a biopsy Decipher score can move the pt across the favorable/unfavorable line that frames the RT plus ADT discussion; it does not establish that treating to the new tier changes metastasis or survival.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Retrospective** development (training n=756, RP genomic data) and validation (n=235, **biopsy** genomic data) with competing-risks DM estimates; training median follow-up **8 years**. Two prospective cohorts (n=4,960 RP; n=977 biopsy) used for **reclassification only**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **Localized prostate cancer** across NCCN low to high/very-high risk. Training cohort second-line therapy included adjuvant RT 7%, salvage RT 13%, salvage ADT 18%.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary outcome: distant metastasis** at 10 years; PCSM secondary. Discrimination by time-dependent c-index; reclassification vs NCCN three-, four- and six-tier systems.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Clinical-genomic tiers separated DM where NCCN fav-int and unfav-int did not split from their neighbors; c-index **0.77 vs 0.68** for NCCN four-tier in training.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Benchmarked against **NCCN** risk groups and **CAPRA** (continuous score 0.68, groups 0.64 in training), both outperformed on DM discrimination. The authors frame NCCN as built to predict biochemical recurrence, which ICECaP found is not a surrogate for survival.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents localized prostate cancer with a Decipher result from RP or biopsy tissue, NCCN low through high risk. Does not represent node-positive or metastatic disease, or a population in which reclassification has been shown to change treatment benefit.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Adjusting for ADT and RT cuts clinical-genomic HRs from **9.3 and 21.9 to 3.5 and 6.1**, so part of the gradient tracks treatment received. Training specimens date from 1997-2004, and many authors are GenomeDx employees.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The system turns a continuous classifier score into categories that fit existing NCCN-based decision rules, which is its practical value. It **does not answer** whether treatment intensification or de-intensification by the new tier changes outcomes.

studies.interpretation:
The core argument of this paper is less that Decipher adds prognostic information, which earlier work had already suggested, and more that a continuous genomic score is clinically inert unless it maps onto the categories treatment recommendations are written in. Collapsing NCCN points and Decipher points into a 0 to 5 scale is a pragmatic answer to that, and the training data show why it was worth attempting: in this RP cohort the NCCN four-tier system did not distinguish low from favorable-intermediate risk (HR 1.2, 95% CI 0.5 to 3.0) or unfavorable-intermediate from high risk (10-year DM 38.0% vs 39.5%). A risk system whose middle boundaries carry little prognostic separation for metastasis is a weak foundation for decisions such as whether to add ADT to RT, and the clinical-genomic tiers spread DM from 3.5% to 54.6%.

The discrimination headline deserves a closer read. The abstract sets the clinical-genomic c-index of 0.84 against NCCN, but 0.84 comes from the 235-patient biopsy validation cohort with a confidence interval of 0.61 to 0.93. The within-cohort comparison in training, 0.77 for the six-tier system vs 0.68 for NCCN four-tier, is the fairer contrast and still favors the new system, but by a smaller margin than the abstract implies. The validation hazard ratios, with upper bounds of 2,727.6 and 7,969.6, reflect a low-risk group with no metastatic events at 10 years; that is reassuring directionally and nearly uninformative about magnitude.

The more important methodological signal is in the treatment-adjusted model. Once ADT, RT and institution are accounted for in training, the intermediate and high clinical-genomic HRs fall from 9.3 and 21.9 to 3.5 and 6.1. They remain significant, and the NCCN HRs shrink too (to 2.5 for both unfavorable-intermediate and high), so the relative advantage holds. But it means part of the raw gradient reflects who received salvage and adjuvant therapy, and a reader should anchor on the adjusted magnitudes when explaining risk to a patient.

For a radiation oncologist, the most relevant finding is where reclassification concentrates. In the large prospective RP cohort, 56.8% of NCCN favorable-intermediate and 36.0% of unfavorable-intermediate patients moved tier, which is exactly the boundary that frames short-course ADT with RT. The training set, however, is post-prostatectomy tissue from 1997 to 2004, and the biopsy validation cohort that mirrors a pre-RT decision is small. The prospective cohorts contribute reclassification counts but no outcomes, so the 30% figure describes how often the label changes, not how often the label change is correct.

What the study cannot settle is prediction. A prognostic tier tells you baseline risk; it does not tell you that a reclassified favorable-intermediate patient benefits from ADT, or that a reclassified unfavorable-intermediate patient can safely omit it. That requires randomized data stratified or selected by the score. The extensive author employment by the manufacturer does not invalidate the analysis but argues for independent replication, ideally in biopsy cohorts treated with contemporary RT.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Biopsy-based validation (n=235) is the pre-RT setting: 10y DM 0%/25.9%/55.2% by tier. Reclassification concentrates at the favorable/unfavorable intermediate split (56.8% and 36.0% moved), the boundary that gates ADT with RT, though adjusted HRs shrink to 3.5 and 6.1 once ADT and RT are modeled.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: Training was on RP specimens, 476 (63%) treated with prostatectomy alone, 8-yr median f/u. NCCN low vs fav-int did not differ for DM (HR 1.2), while clinical-genomic high reached 54.6% 10y DM; in the prospective RP cohort 27.2% of NCCN high-risk were reclassified.

open_questions: Does genomic reclassification predict ADT benefit with RT?
Independent validation in larger biopsy-based cohorts

related_trials.brief_title: Two Studies for Patients With Unfavorable Intermediate Risk Prostate Cancer Testing Less Intense Treatment for Patients With a Low Gene Risk Score and Testing a More Intense Treatment for Patients With a Higher Gene Risk Score, The Guidance Trial

studies.tldr: 5yr FFS 84% vs 84%, adjusted HR 1.002 (95% CI 0.758-1.325): 42.7 Gy/7 fx non-inferior to 78 Gy/39 fx in intermediate-to-high-risk prostate, no ADT.
details: 🔍 Open-label randomised phase 3 non-inferiority trial, 12 centres in Sweden and Denmark, N=1200 (2005-2015)

details.text: 🔍 Population and eligibility

details.text: 🔍 RT technique

Dose prescribed as mean PTV dose

Gold fiducials: isotropic 7 mm CTV-PTV margin

details.text: 📊 Efficacy and G2+ toxicity by arm (per-protocol)
📊 Cumulative late physician-reported G2+ toxicity

⚠️ Open-label: physician-graded toxicity unblinded, though biochemical relapse assessed blindly

studies.significance: The schedule tested is 42.7 Gy/7 fx every other weekday to a prostate-only CTV (no seminal vesicles) with a 7 mm fiducial margin, 80% 3DCRT, no ADT. That supports UHF for prostate-only volumes without ADT, not SV-inclusive or ADT-paired high-risk plans. Counsel on the 1yr G2+ GU bump (6% vs 2%).
studies.monday_clinic: In a man up to 75 with intermediate-risk, N0M0 prostate cancer, PSA ≤20 and no ADT planned, this supports 7-fraction UHF as disease-control equivalent to 39 fractions; it does not extend to pts needing ADT, PSA >20, or seminal vesicle coverage.

primary_endpoint.name: Failure-free survival (biochemical or clinical failure)
primary_endpoint.stat_detail: adjusted HR 1.002 (95% CI 0.758-1.325), non-inferior vs HR limit 1.338

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Open-label randomised phase 3 non-inferiority** trial, 1:1, 12 centres in Sweden and Denmark, **N=1200** randomised 2005-2015. Median follow-up **5.0 yr** (IQR 3.1-7.0).

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Men up to 75 with **intermediate-to-high-risk, T1c-T3a N0M0** prostate cancer, **PSA ≤20**, WHO PS 0-2. **No ADT allowed.** 89% intermediate risk, 11% high risk.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **42.7 Gy/7 fx** (3 d/wk, 2.5 wk) vs **78.0 Gy/39 fx** (5 d/wk, 8 wk), prescribed as mean PTV dose and designed equi-effective for late effects at α/β = 3 Gy. **CTV prostate only**, no seminal vesicles; 7 mm isotropic margin with fiducials; 80% 3DCRT.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** failure-free survival (Phoenix nadir+2 biochemical or clinical failure), per-protocol, NI margin **4% at 5yr** (critical HR **1.338**). Secondary: OS, PCSS, RTOG toxicity, erectile function.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Efficacy and toxicity by arm are tabulated above; the primary met NI with a point estimate of essentially no difference.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: UHF carries a **higher acute and 1yr GU burden** (G2+ at 1yr 6% vs 2%, p=0.0037) that **converges by 5yr** (5% vs 5%). Late bowel toxicity no different; patient-reported acute urinary and bowel symptoms higher with UHF.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: CHHiP, RTOG 0415, PROFIT and HYPRO established **moderate hypofractionation** against conventional fractionation. HYPO-RT-PC is the first randomised test of **ultra-hypofractionation**, the evidence the 2018 ASTRO/ASCO/AUA guideline said it was waiting for.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents men up to 75 with intermediate-to-high-risk (89% intermediate), N0M0, T1c-T3a prostate cancer, PSA ≤20, treated without ADT. Does not represent pts receiving ADT, PSA >20, or volumes covering seminal vesicles or pelvic nodes.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The upper CI bound (1.325) clears the 1.338 limit **narrowly**. 80% 3DCRT and a 7 mm margin predate modern SBRT delivery, and 7 fx every other weekday is not the 5 fx schedule most programs use. Five-year median follow-up is short for late intermediate-risk failures.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The trial settles **disease-control equivalence of UHF** for prostate-only, ADT-free treatment. It leaves open UHF with ADT, with SV or nodal coverage, and against moderate hypofractionation.

studies.interpretation:
The question HYPO-RT-PC answers is narrower than its headline. Moderate hypofractionation was already established by CHHiP, RTOG 0415, PROFIT and HYPRO, and the 2018 ASTRO/ASCO/AUA guideline still graded ultra-hypofractionation as conditional because no randomised data existed. This trial supplies that randomised comparison, but against dose-escalated conventional fractionation (78 Gy in 39 fractions), not against the moderate schedules most centres had already moved to. A reader choosing between a moderate schedule and an ultra-hypofractionated one gets indirect support here, not a head-to-head answer.

The efficacy result is as clean as non-inferiority results get on the point estimate: identical 5-year failure-free survival of 84% and an adjusted HR of 1.002. The confidence interval tells a more careful story. Its upper bound of 1.325 sits just below the prespecified limit of 1.338, so the data rule out a meaningful disadvantage only by a small cushion. The margin itself was set after the trial was converted from a superiority design, prompted by a blinded interim that estimated 87% failure-free survival overall. Because that interim was blinded to arm, the redesign does not look like outcome-driven goalpost moving, but the reader should know the 4% margin was chosen mid-course. The per-protocol primary is a common worry in non-inferiority trials, since it can flatter equivalence; here the per-protocol and ITT populations differ by 10 pts, so that concern is close to moot.

Transferability is where the RT details matter most. The schedule was 42.7 Gy in 7 fractions given three days a week, prescribed to the mean PTV dose, to a prostate-only CTV that excluded the seminal vesicles, with a 7 mm isotropic margin and 3DCRT in 80% of pts. That is not the five-fraction SBRT most programs deliver today, and the direction of the difference cuts both ways: tighter modern margins and IMRT should reduce toxicity, while a higher dose per fraction and a shorter course could raise it. The absence of ADT and the small high-risk fraction (11%) mean the result says little about unfavourable disease where ADT or seminal vesicle coverage is standard.

The toxicity pattern deserves a specific counselling conversation rather than a summary of equivalence. UHF produced more acute urinary morbidity and a real bump in grade 2 or worse urinary toxicity at one year (6% vs 2%), and cumulative late urinary toxicity at two years ran 13% vs 9% before converging to 18% vs 17% at five years. Toxicity grading was unblinded, though patient-reported outcomes moved in the same direction, which makes the signal more believable rather than less.

What would make the conclusion wrong is late biochemical failure. Median follow-up of five years is short for an intermediate-risk population, and prostate cancer deaths (11 vs 8) are too few to read. The decision this moves is fraction number for prostate-only, ADT-free treatment; it does not settle ultra-hypofractionation with ADT, with elective volumes, or against moderate hypofractionation.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The schedule tested is 42.7 Gy/7 fx every other weekday to a prostate-only CTV (no seminal vesicles) with a 7 mm fiducial margin, 80% 3DCRT, no ADT. That supports UHF for prostate-only volumes without ADT, not SV-inclusive or ADT-paired high-risk plans. Counsel on the 1yr G2+ GU bump (6% vs 2%).

studies.tldr: Crude LRR 4.7% at median 5.6y after mastectomy without PMRT in T1-T2N0 with ≥1 high-risk feature; only tumor size predicted LRR (HR 1.70).
details: 🔍 Single-institution (MSKCC) retrospective cohort, mastectomies 2006-2011
🔍 N=672 T1-T2N0 with ≥1 high-risk feature; 15 who received PMRT excluded, leaving 657

details.text: 🔍 High-risk features defined by the authors

details: 🔍 98% SLNB alone; 86% received adjuvant systemic therapy
📊 LRR 4.7% (31 pts) at median 5.6y; median time to LRR 33 mo

details.text: 📊 Local recurrence 2.6% (17 pts), regional recurrence 2.6% (17 pts)

details: 📐 Tumor size (continuous) predicted LRR: HR 1.70 (95% CI 1.26-2.29), P=.006
📐 Systemic therapy reduced LRR: HR 0.40 (95% CI 0.17-0.92), P=.03
📊 Age, grade, LVI, multifocality, location: not associated with LRR (all P>.05)
📊 LRR by number of high-risk features (log-rank P=.54)

details.text: 📊 Site of LRR (31 events)
⚠️ 8 of 22 isolated LRRs were axilla-only, 7 after SLNB alone; authors suspect false-negative SLNB
⚠️ 10 of 31 LRR pts (32%) did not receive recommended systemic therapy

details: ⚠️ ≥4-feature subgroup small; the 9.4% crude rate has a wide CI (0.71-0.98)
🔗 vs EORTC 22922: regional recurrence 2.7% vs 4.2% with nodal RT; this cohort 2.6% regional without any RT
⚠️ High-volume dedicated breast surgeons; generalizability uncertain per authors

verdict.rationale: Single-institution retrospective series with no PMRT comparator; describes baseline LRR risk, cannot estimate PMRT benefit. Small ≥4-feature subgroup limits the null risk-factor finding.
verdict.audience: T1-T2N0 breast, mastectomy + SLNB, ≥1 high-risk feature, no PMRT

studies.significance: Regional failure without any RT was 2.6%, already below the 4.2% control-arm regional rate in EORTC 22922, which leaves little room for nodal or chest wall RT to add benefit in this group. Tumor size is the one feature that held up (HR 1.70 continuous). Note that axilla-only failures after SLNB alone were overrepresented.
studies.monday_clinic: In T1-T2N0 post-mastectomy pts getting indicated systemic therapy, LVI, age <40, multifocality, high grade or medial location alone do not support PMRT referral in this series; it does not address T2 tumors with several features, where data were sparse.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Single-institution **retrospective** cohort at MSKCC, mastectomies January 2006 to December 2011. **Median follow-up 5.6y**. LRR defined as biopsy-proven ipsilateral chest wall or axillary, internal mammary or supraclavicular recurrence.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **T1-T2N0** invasive breast cancer with **≥1 high-risk feature** (age <40y, multifocal/multicentric, LVI, medial/central location, high nuclear grade). N0 meant no tumor in the SLNs, including ITCs and micrometastases. Neoadjuvant chemo, bilateral and recurrent disease excluded; 15 PMRT pts excluded, leaving 657.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: 98% had SLNB alone. **86% received adjuvant systemic therapy**: 41% chemo plus endocrine, 14% chemo alone, 32% endocrine alone. 70% of HER2+ pts got trastuzumab.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **No PMRT** in the analyzed cohort. Only 15 of 672 (2%) received PMRT over the study period, so no RT comparator exists.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **LRR 4.7%** (31 pts), local and regional each 2.6%. **Tumor size HR 1.70** (95% CI 1.26-2.29); **systemic therapy HR 0.40** (95% CI 0.17-0.92). Number of risk factors **not associated** with LRR (P=.54).

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: EORTC 22922 and MA.20 showed DFS benefit from regional nodal RT in populations that included high-risk N0 disease; per the source, N0 made up 10% of MA.20 and 44% of EORTC. The regional recurrence here without RT (2.6%) sits below the EORTC 22922 control arm (4.2%). SUPREMO, which includes high-risk N0 pts, is the randomized test of this question.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents T1-T2N0 pts after mastectomy with SLNB, at least one conventional high-risk feature, and modern adjuvant systemic therapy. Does not represent pts after neoadjuvant chemo, T3 or node-positive disease, or pts who decline systemic therapy.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Only 32 pts had 4-5 features (Fig 1), so the null risk-count finding is underpowered where it matters most. Surgery was done by high-volume breast surgeons, and axilla-only failures after SLNB suggest a false-negative contribution not addressed by PMRT decisions alone.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Authors attribute the low LRR to contemporary systemic therapy and argue conventional features **do not by themselves mandate PMRT**. The data establish baseline risk without RT, not the size of any PMRT benefit, so the question for T2 tumors carrying several features stays open.

studies.interpretation:
The value of this series is that it measures the untreated baseline. Most of what the field believed about high-risk node-negative disease after mastectomy came from cohorts treated in the 1980s to early 2000s, when far fewer pts received adjuvant systemic therapy and HER2-directed therapy was not routine. The authors report 86% systemic therapy use against the 38% to 77% they cite for older series, and a crude LRR of 4.7% against historical figures as high as 20% in pts with multiple features. If the baseline has fallen that far, any proportional benefit from PMRT now buys a much smaller absolute gain, and that is the real argument of the paper.

The comparison with the nodal irradiation trials makes the same point from a different direction. EORTC 22922 and MA.20 are the evidence usually invoked to justify regional RT in high-risk N0 disease, yet node-negative pts were a minority of MA.20 and EORTC enrolled mostly breast-conserving surgery. The regional recurrence here with no RT at all, 2.6%, falls below the 4.2% the source quotes for the EORTC 22922 control arm. Cross-series comparison of this kind is weak, since definitions, follow-up and populations differ, but it does suggest the trial-derived benefit should not be ported directly onto a modern mastectomy population with negative SLNs on careful serial sectioning.

The methodological limits should move confidence in specific ways. First, this is a cohort with no RT arm, so it cannot say what PMRT would have prevented; it can only say what happens without it. Second, the headline negative finding, that counting risk factors does not stratify LRR, rests on a log-rank test across groups where the highest-risk stratum had only 32 pts. The crude rate there was 9.4% with a lower 5-year LRR-free bound of 0.71, which is not reassurance; it is an unresolved estimate. A reader should treat "features do not matter" as "features could not be shown to matter in this sample." Third, the risk score weights five heterogeneous features equally, which can dilute a genuine signal from any one of them. Tumor size, the one variable analyzed continuously, was the one that came through (HR 1.70), and that may partly reflect the greater statistical power of a continuous term.

The pattern of failure deserves more attention than the abstract gives it. Eight of 22 isolated LRRs were axilla-only, and 7 of those 8 followed SLNB alone. The authors suspect false-negative SLNB. That is a surgical staging issue, and chest wall-directed RT would not address it, while comprehensive nodal RT might. This is a reminder that a low aggregate LRR can hide a failure mode that one specific RT field would target.

The systemic therapy association (HR 0.40) is real-world and confounded by indication, and a third of pts who failed had not received recommended systemic therapy. For an RT decision, the practical read is that the low baseline applies to pts actually receiving indicated systemic treatment. The paper supports not referring T1-T2N0 pts for PMRT on the strength of LVI, age, grade, multifocality or medial location alone. It leaves open T2 tumors carrying several features, and those are the pts SUPREMO's node-negative subset is positioned to inform.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Regional failure without RT was 2.6%, below the 4.2% EORTC 22922 control-arm regional rate, so nodal RT in high-risk N0 post-mastectomy has little absolute room to work. Tumor size (HR 1.70) is the only feature that predicted LRR, which argues for weighting size over feature counting when weighing PMRT for T2N0.

papers.title: Development and Validation of a Novel Integrated Clinical-Genomic Risk Group Classification for Localized Prostate Cancer
papers.abstract: Purpose It is clinically challenging to integrate genomic-classifier results that report a numeric risk of recurrence into treatment recommendations for localized prostate cancer, which are founded in the framework of risk groups. We aimed to develop a novel clinical-genomic risk grouping system that can readily be incorporated into treatment guidelines for localized prostate cancer. Materials and Methods Two multicenter cohorts (n = 991) were used for training and validation of the clinical-genomic risk groups, and two additional cohorts (n = 5,937) were used for reclassification analyses. Competing risks analysis was used to estimate the risk of distant metastasis. Time-dependent c-indices were constructed to compare clinicopathologic risk models with the clinical-genomic risk groups. Results With a median follow-up of 8 years for patients in the training cohort, 10-year distant metastasis rates for National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) low, favorable-intermediate, unfavorable-intermediate, and high-risk were 7.3%, 9.2%, 38.0%, and 39.5%, respectively. In contrast, the three-tier clinical-genomic risk groups had 10-year distant metastasis rates of 3.5%, 29.4%, and 54.6%, for low-, intermediate-, and high-risk, respectively, which were consistent in the validation cohort (0%, 25.9%, and 55.2%, respectively). C-indices for the clinical-genomic risk grouping system (0.84; 95% CI, 0.61 to 0.93) were improved over NCCN (0.73; 95% CI, 0.60 to 0.86) and Cancer of the Prostate Risk Assessment (0.74; 95% CI, 0.65 to 0.84), and 30% of patients using NCCN low/intermediate/high would be reclassified by the new three-tier system and 67% of patients would be reclassified from NCCN six-tier (very-low– to very-high–risk) by the new six-tier system. Conclusion A commercially available genomic classifier in combination with standard clinicopathologic variables can generate a simple-to-use clinical-genomic risk grouping that more accurately identifies patients at low, intermediate, and high risk for metastasis and can be easily incorporated into current guidelines to better risk-stratify patients.

Ten-Year Outcomes of Moderately Hypofractionated (70 Gy in 28 fractions) Intensity Modulated Radiation Therapy for Localized Prostate Cancer
Tolerance doses for late adverse events after hypofractionated radiotherapy for prostate cancer on trial NRG Oncology/RTOG 0415
Are there patients with T1 to T2, lymph node‐negative breast cancer who are “high‐risk” for locoregional disease recurrence?
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND Indications for postmastectomy radiotherapy (PMRT) in patients with T1 to T2, lymph node‐negative (N0) breast cancer with “high‐risk” features are controversial. The European Organization for Research and Treatment of Cancer (EORTC) 22922 and National Cancer Institute of Canada Clinical Trials Group MA20 trials reporting improved 10‐year disease‐free survival with lymph node irradiation included patients with high‐risk N0 disease, but, to the authors’ knowledge, benefits in patients receiving modern systemic therapy are uncertain. METHODS The authors retrospectively identified patients with T1 to T2N0 disease who were treated with mastectomy from January 2006 through December 2011. High‐risk features included age <40 years, multifocality/multicentricity, lymphovascular invasion, medial/central tumor location, and high nuclear grade. RESULTS Among 672 eligible patients, only 15 received PMRT and were excluded. Of the remaining 657 patients, 187 (28%) had 1 high‐risk feature and 449 patients (68%) had ≥ 2 high‐risk features. A total of 36 patients with unknown tumor grade were excluded from risk analysis. Approximately 98% of patients underwent sentinel lymph node biopsy alone and 86% received adjuvant systemic therapy. At a median of 5.6 years of follow‐up, the locoregional disease recurrence (LRR) rate was 4.7% (31 patients). Increasing tumor size was found to be associated with LRR (hazard ratio, 1.70; P = .006), whereas other high‐risk features were not (all P > .05). Receipt of systemic therapy decreased the LRR rate (hazard ratio, 0.40; P = .03). Although crude LRR rates increased from 3.8% to 9.4% with 1 versus ≥ 4 high‐risk features, the number of risk factors was not found to be significantly associated with LRR ( P = .54). CONCLUSIONS In the current study, a low crude LRR rate (4.7%) was observed in a large unselected cohort of patients with T1 to T2N0 breast cancer with high‐risk features who were treated with mastectomy and systemic therapy without PMRT. Although increasing tumor size and the omission of systemic therapy were found to be predictive, other features did not confer a higher LRR risk either independently or together, and do not by themselves mandate the use of PMRT in this patient population.
